assessment.rationale: A 3:00 marathon means holding about 6:52 per mile for 26.2 miles, and runners who do that usually build to 50-70 miles a week. Starting from 20 miles a week and an 8-mile long run, 12 weeks on 4 days a week is only enough to reach about 36 miles a week safely, so aim for about 3:45 and adjust once a tune-up race or long-run paces show your actual fitness.

critiques: week 5 jumps mileage >20% (21→26)
week 8 jumps mileage >20% (25→32)

The long run takes too large a share of weekly volume in the peak block: 16 of 32 mi (50%), 18 of 34 (53%) and 20 of 36 (56%). The usual ceiling is about 30-35%, and going past it on 4 runs a week raises injury risk.

The long run grows from 8 to 20 mi in 10 weeks on a base of only 20 mpw, and the 20-miler includes 4-5 mi at goal pace on hills. For this volume that is aggressive. A 16-18 mi cap, or keeping the 20 at easy effort, would be safer.

Weeks 8-10 have too many hard days. Week 8 puts a tempo, a long run with marathon-pace miles and downhill repeats into a 4-run week. Week 9 has 6 mi at marathon pace, a long run with hills at marathon effort and a hot-day pace run. That leaves almost no easy running between hard sessions.
Weekly volume jumps 28% from week 7 to week 8 (25 to 32 mi). That comes straight after a step-back week and together with the first 16-miler and the new downhill repeats.

Hard downhill repeats in week 8 and the hill work on top of a 16-20 mi long run put a lot of eccentric load on quads in a low-mileage runner. Downhill volume should come in more gradually, with only one hill-focused session a week.

A peak of 36 mpw is thin for an 8:35/mi (about 3:45) marathon goal, and the late-race pace may not hold. The cool-weather goal is optimistic unless the runner has previous marathon or half-marathon results to support it.
Week 8 says 4 mi at marathon pace but places it in miles 11-15, which is 5 miles. One of the two numbers needs correcting.
Week 9 to 10 raises weekly mileage from 32 to 37 (about 16%) and the long run from 13 to 15 mi in the same week; spread the jump over two weeks or cap week 10 near 35 mi
The 15 mi long run is about 40% of a 37 mi week, which is a heavy share of weekly load; trim it to 14 mi or add an easy mile or two elsewhere
Week 10 puts the peak volume, the longest run and a rolling-hill course in one week, right after week 9's downhill repeats; drop the cruise intervals or make them shorter that week
A 37 mi peak and a 15 mi longest run are thin preparation for 26.2 mi, so the 8:35/mi goal is optimistic unless the week-8 10K clearly supports it; the plan should default to the slower band
Week 8 is labeled a step-back week but includes an all-out 10K and a 10 mi long run; schedule the long run at least 3 days after the time trial or shorten it to 8 mi
week 9 jumps mileage >20% (25→33)
The longest run is 14 mi (week 10), which leaves a 12+ mi gap to 26.2. For a 36 mi peak week, aim for at least one 16-18 mi run in weeks 9-10, or expect the late miles of the race to be very hard.
Peak volume is only 36 mi, and only one week tops 33 mi. That is thin support for an 8:35-9:00/mi marathon goal, so the default pace band may be too optimistic.
Week 10's focus says the long run and the hills are the only hard work, but no hill session is listed that week. The note contradicts the session list.

assessment.rationale: A 3:30 marathon means about 8:01 per mile, and most runners who hit that are doing 40 to 55 miles a week for several months; going from 25 to that range in 10 weeks raises injury risk, and the NYC bridges add time. If you build to around 40 miles a week with long runs of 18 to 20 miles, 3:50 to 4:00 is a realistic target, and you can adjust it after a tune-up half marathon around week 6.

critiques: week 5 jumps mileage >20% (27→34)
Long runs take up 45-50% of weekly mileage every week (12 of 25, 16 of 34, 20 of 40). On 5 runs a week that is lopsided. Keep long runs nearer 30-35% of weekly volume, or raise the weekday mileage.
A 40 mpw peak is thin support for a 20 mi run with 6 miles at marathon effort. That one session is half of the week's mileage.
Week 1 opens with a 12 mi long run at 25 mpw, and the plan never states the runner's current base. That start is only safe if they already run 12 mi regularly.

Weeks 5-8 put marathon-effort or hill work into every long run, on top of a second session of intervals, hill repeats or tempo. That is two hard days a week for four weeks in a row with no easy long run in between.

Week 6 puts hill repeats with fast downhills and an 18 mi run with 5 hilly marathon-effort miles in the same week. Together that is a big eccentric load on the quads at the plan's highest-intensity point.
The 10-week build is short. It ramps from 25 to 40 mpw with only one step-back week (week 4), leaving little room to absorb a missed week or a minor injury.

assessment.rationale: A 3:10 marathon means holding 7:15/mile for 26.2 miles, and most runners who manage that have built up to 55-65 miles a week and can show a recent half marathon around 1:30; at 35 miles a week with no race result to point to, 18 weeks isn't enough to close that gap safely. Aim for 3:30 (about 8:00/mile) and build gradually to a 50-mile peak week, and if a tune-up half in weeks 10-12 comes in under 1:33, move the target toward 3:15-3:20.

critiques: The long run takes up about 40-43% of weekly mileage almost every week (14 of 35 in week 1, 20 of 48 in week 12, 21 of 50 in week 15). Most plans keep it nearer 30-35%, so either add easy mileage on other days or trim the long runs a little.

Week 11 is called a step-back week but has a 5 mi tempo and an optional tune-up half marathon raced at 1:39. That is two hard efforts in a recovery week; drop the tempo or make it easy if the half goes ahead.

Weeks 13 and 15 put 10 mi (2x5) and 8 mi of marathon pace into 20-21 mi long runs, on top of a 5x1 mi or 6x1000m session in the same week. Back-to-back peak weeks with that load leave little margin; space the VO2 session at least 3 days from the long run, or cut a rep.

Week 1 starts at 35 mi with a 14 mi long run and steady-pace work, which assumes the runner is already at about 30-35 mi/week with long runs of 12 mi or more. If they are not, the first 2-3 weeks ramp too fast.
week 5 jumps mileage >20% (30→38)
week 9 jumps mileage >20% (38→47)
week 12 jumps mileage >20% (42→54)
week 15 jumps mileage >20% (48→58)

The threshold paces (7:20-7:30/mi) and the 6:55/mi 1000m reps are about 15-25 s/mi faster than a 3:30 marathon fitness level supports. Daniels-style tables put threshold near 7:45-7:50/mi for that goal, so these sessions risk turning into race efforts. Base them on a recent race or on the week 11 half result.

The week 15 long run is 20 of 52 miles (about 38% of the week) and includes 7 mi at marathon pace. That is a heavy single session for a runner who started at 25-30 mi/week; cap the marathon-pace miles at 5-6 or add easy volume elsewhere in the week.

Weeks 10 and 12 each pair a threshold or VO2 session with a separate midweek 5 mi marathon-pace run and a 16-17 mi long run. That makes three demanding days in a 46 mi week; make one of the midweek sessions easy or move the marathon-pace miles into the long run.

Peaking at 52 mi/week from a 25-30 mi base is a modest load for a 3:30 goal. The plan never checks whether that goal is realistic before week 16 sets an 8:00/mi race plan. Use the week 11 half (1:39 predicts about 3:25-3:30) to confirm or adjust the goal, and give a fallback pace if the runner skips the half.

assessment.rationale: A 3:00:00 marathon requires holding 6:52 per mile for 26.2 miles, which usually takes months of 50+ mile weeks; from a base of 20 miles per week and an 8-mile long run, 12 weeks on 4 days per week is only enough to build safely to about 36 miles per week with a 20-mile long run. A goal of about 4:15 is realistic for this build, and the runner can adjust it after a tune-up half marathon around week 8.

critiques: week 5 jumps mileage >20% (20→26)
week 8 jumps mileage >20% (25→32)

Long runs take too large a share of weekly volume: 18 of 32 mi in week 8 (56%) and 20 of 36 mi in week 9 (56%). Most plans keep the long run near 30-40% of the week; on a 4-day schedule the other three runs are too short to support the long ones.
The long run jumps from 12 mi (week 7) to 18 mi (week 8), and the previous longest was 14 mi in week 6. Add a 16-mi step or move the 18 later.
Peak volume of 36 mi/week is thin support for a 20-miler and a 26.2 mi race. A runner at 10:30-11:00/mi will be out for about 3.5 hours on the 20-miler with little weekly mileage behind it.

The week 8 long run has 10:00/mi for the first 6 mi, which is faster than the stated easy range of 10:45-11:30/mi. It also has 5 mi at marathon pace (miles 13-17) in the plan's first 18-miler. That is too much stress for one run at this volume.

Week 8 pairs that hard 18-miler with a downhill and tired-legs uphill session, so 2 of the week's 4 runs are hard. The same happens in week 9: a 4 mi tempo plus a 20-miler with hills at miles 16-19 and a race-pace finish.
Week 7 is labeled a step-back week but still has two quality sessions (1 km repeats and downhill repeats) plus a 12-mi long run. Cut it to one quality session.
Week 6 combines a tempo with marathon-pace miles at the end of a long run that starts downhill, and it is also the first heat-training week. Hard days and new stressors are bunched together.
Week 10 is a taper week but still has a 12-mi long run, a 4 mi marathon-pace session and a heat-layer run. Cutting 28 from 36 mi is fine, but the intensity is not reduced.
The race-day note to 'drink at every station' in the heat risks hyponatremia for a slower runner on course 4+ hours. Base drinking on the week 10 sweat-rate test and thirst, and include sodium.

The plan has 12 weeks with a low base (20 mi/week at the start). That is a tight timeline for Boston's downhill course. The downhill work helps, but the volume ramp and long-run progression leave little margin if a week is missed.
Week 8 to week 9 raises weekly mileage from 33 to 39 (about 18%) and the long run from 15 to 18 mi in the same week. That is the largest jump in the plan, and it lands in the peak week.

The long run takes too large a share of weekly volume on only 4-5 running days: 8 of 20 mi (40%) in week 1, 13 of 30 (43%) in week 6 and 18 of 39 (46%) in week 9. Most guidance keeps it nearer 30-35%.

Week 7 is labeled a step-back week, but mileage only drops from 30 to 28 (about 7%). It also adds downhill repeats at marathon-pace effort and starts heat work, so it gives little real recovery before the peak block.

Starting at 20 mpw and peaking at 39 mpw in 12 weeks is a thin base for Boston's downhill course. The 18 mi cap is sensible, but the later miles of the race carry more risk, and the plan could state that more plainly in its pacing advice.

Downhill work at marathon-pace effort appears in weeks 7 and 11 with only light preparation in week 2. Eccentric quad load at that effort can leave lasting soreness, so keep it short and stop it at the first sign of soreness.

assessment.rationale: A 3:30 marathon means holding 8:01 per mile for 26.2 miles, which usually takes 45 to 55 miles a week for several months, and NYC's bridges and late climb in Central Park add time on top of that. Building from 25 to about 40 miles a week over 10 weeks, with long runs up to 18 to 20 miles, makes 3:50 to 4:00 a realistic target; a recent half marathon under 1:40 would be a reason to revise it.

critiques: week 5 jumps mileage >20% (26→33)

Long runs make up 47-50% of weekly mileage in every week (for example 12 of 25 mi in week 1 and 20 of 40 mi in week 7). The usual guideline is about 30-35%, so the rest of the week is too thin to support these long runs and injury risk goes up.
A 20 mi long run on a 40 mi peak week is too long for the volume. Either raise peak weekly mileage to the mid-40s or higher, or cap the long run at about 16-18 mi.
Week 1 opens with a 12 mi long run at 25 mi/week. That only works if the runner already handles about 10-12 mi long runs comfortably; the plan doesn't state that baseline.

Weeks 5-7 put two hard sessions in each 5-day week: a tempo or threshold workout plus a long run with 5-6 mi at marathon pace and hills. With half the weekly volume in the long run, that's a lot of intensity for a 33-40 mi/week runner. Consider making some long runs fully easy.
The 10-week build has only one step-back week (week 4), then three straight weeks of increases to the peak. That's short for a marathon build at this mileage.
Week 4 is labeled Build but is a step-back week. It's a minor labeling inconsistency.
Long run takes too large a share of weekly volume: the week 8 long run is 16 of 39 mi (about 41%), and weeks 5, 6 and 9 are about 37%, which puts a lot of load on one day
The peak long run of 16 mi, with only one run over 14 mi and a peak week of 39 mi, is thin for a full marathon; expect a hard final 10 km, especially on the NYC bridges and Fifth Ave
The 8:58/mi goal pace (about a 3:55 finish) is ambitious on a 10-week build that peaks at 39 mi/week; treat it as an effort target and be ready to slow down
Taper week 9 still has two quality sessions (3 x 1 mi at 8:45 and a marathon-pace finish to the long run); dropping one would leave fresher legs for race week
week 5 jumps mileage >20% (33→42)
week 8 jumps mileage >20% (38→50)

Week 7 to week 8 jumps from 38 to 50 mi (+32%) and adds the longest run with 5 mi at marathon effort in the same week. Week 6 already reached 46 mi, so the load is not new, but trimming week 8 to about 46-48 mi would lower the injury risk for a runner who started near 30 mi/week.

The whole build is 10 weeks from a 28-30 mi/week base, with only three runs of 14 mi or more before a hilly course. That is tight. The plan's own advice to treat 8:58/mi as an effort target and fall back to 9:10-9:20/mi if needed is necessary, not optional.
Week 10 lists long_run_miles as 5 and weekly_miles as 16, but the race is in that week's sessions. The fields should say whether the 26.2 mi race is counted.
